items.title: What we actually run: Apache, certbot, PM2 and Cloudflare
items.body: Our three live apps (gglearn, ggsocial, ggmoney) run on one VPS and share the same shape. A Next.js app (or, for ggmoney, PHP served through Apache) is started by PM2, which restarts it if it dies and brings it back after a reboot once `pm2 save` has been run. The app listens only on 127.0.0.1 (gglearn on port 3400, ggsocial on 3200), so nothing can reach it directly. Apache is the reverse proxy: a vhost uses ProxyPass and ProxyPassReverse to forward to that local port. TLS certificates come from Let's Encrypt through certbot, which also creates the port-443 vhost file and renews it. In front of everything sits Cloudflare. gglearn keeps deploy/apache-cloudflare-only.conf, generated by update-cloudflare-ips.sh from Cloudflare's published address ranges, so only Cloudflare (and the machine itself) may connect; this stops anyone bypassing Cloudflare and spoofing the X-Forwarded-For header the app uses to find the client address. The script refuses to write an implausible list, because an empty allow-list would lock everyone out. ggmoney's DEPLOY.md asks for Cloudflare SSL mode Full (strict), because HMRC tokens cross the Cloudflare-to-origin hop. ggsocial's notes warn that the live :443 vhost is a copy in sites-enabled, not a symlink, so edit that copy and run apachectl configtest before reloading. Nginx, Terraform and Kubernetes are not part of this production path.

questions.prompt: On the production VPS, which program acts as the reverse proxy in front of the gglearn and ggsocial Node apps?

options.text: Apache, using ProxyPass to a local port
Nginx, using proxy_pass
Cloudflare alone, with no server-side proxy
PM2, which routes requests by hostname

questions.prompt: Why do the Node apps listen only on 127.0.0.1?

options.text: Because PM2 cannot bind to public addresses
Because Cloudflare requires it for certificates
To make the app start faster
So they can only be reached through the proxy, not directly from the internet

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of deploy/apache-cloudflare-only.conf?

options.text: Issue the TLS certificate for the site
Cache static files at the edge
Allow only Cloudflare and the local machine to connect, so client IPs from X-Forwarded-For cannot be spoofed
Restart Apache after each deploy

questions.prompt: Explain why update-cloudflare-ips.sh checks the downloaded address lists before writing the config, and what could go wrong without that check.
questions.answer: If the fetch failed or returned junk, the script could write an empty or wrong allow-list. Because the config only permits listed addresses, an empty list would block every visitor, including Cloudflare, taking the site down. The script checks the lists look like valid IPv4 and IPv6 ranges and exits without writing otherwise.
questions.rubric: Mentions a bad or empty fetch; says allow-list means everyone is locked out; says the script refuses to write rather than writing a bad file.

items.title: Deploying with a script and GitHub Actions: gglearn's deploy.yml
items.body: gglearn has one real GitHub Actions workflow, .github/workflows/deploy.yml. It runs on every push to main and can also be started by hand (workflow_dispatch). A concurrency group called deploy with cancel-in-progress set to false means two deploys never overlap and a running one is not cancelled by a newer push. The job first checks that the repository secrets DEPLOY_SSH_KEY, DEPLOY_HOST, DEPLOY_USER and DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS exist and fails with a clear message if one is missing. It then writes an ssh config with the alias gglink-live and StrictHostKeyChecking yes, and runs bash deploy/deploy.sh. That script rsyncs the code to the server, excluding node_modules, .next, .git, database files and .env files, then over ssh takes a flock lock so only one deploy runs at a time, runs npm ci, drizzle-kit push, npm run build, pm2 startOrRestart and pm2 save, and finally polls http://127.0.0.1:3400/ up to ten times and fails the deploy if it never returns 200. drizzle-kit push deliberately has no --force, so a schema change that would delete rows stops the deploy. Note what is missing: this workflow runs no tests or lint, and gglearn has no test script. ggsocial and ggmoney have no .github folder; ggsocial deploys from a developer machine with scripts/deploy.sh, which type-checks, lints and tests first.

questions.prompt: When does gglearn's deploy workflow run?

options.text: Only on pull requests
On every push to main, and manually via workflow_dispatch
Only on a nightly schedule
Only when a release tag is created

questions.prompt: What does concurrency with cancel-in-progress set to false do in this workflow?

options.text: Queues deploys so they never overlap and does not cancel one that is already running
Cancels the running deploy whenever a new push arrives
Runs every deploy in parallel for speed
Disables the workflow on weekends

questions.prompt: Why does deploy.sh run drizzle-kit push without --force?

options.text: Because --force is not supported by SQLite
Because it makes the build faster
Because PM2 needs the schema unchanged
So a schema change that would delete rows fails the deploy instead of running silently

questions.prompt: Describe the safety checks in gglearn's deploy path, and name one gap compared with what ggsocial's deploy script does.
questions.answer: Checks: required secrets verified up front; strict host key checking; concurrency group plus a server-side flock so deploys do not overlap; no --force on drizzle push; a post-deploy health poll that fails the deploy if the app does not return 200. Gap: the workflow runs no tests, lint or type check (and gglearn has no test script), whereas ggsocial's scripts/deploy.sh type-checks, lints and tests before sending anything.
questions.rubric: Names at least three real checks; identifies the missing test/lint step in gglearn's workflow; refers to ggsocial's pre-deploy checks.

items.title: Docker Compose and CI in the Moksy platform
items.body: Moksy is a set of microservices, and Docker Compose is how it is run. The repo has docker-compose.yml plus overlays: prod, staging, release and registry. It defines two networks, moksy-public and moksy-internal, and the internal one is marked internal: true, so containers on it have no route to the outside world. Services use restart: unless-stopped, with a comment explaining why: a process that exits with code 0 is not a failure, so on-failure would never bring it back. The dashboard's production image is a multi-stage build: a node stage compiles the Vite app, and only the compiled dist is copied into a small nginx image, whose nginx.conf serves static files and sets long immutable caching on /assets/ but no-cache on index.html. So Nginx is used here, but only as a static file server inside a container. Moksy has two GitHub workflows. ci.yml runs on pushes and pull requests with a real Mongo service container and jobs for lint, unit and integration tests, a Compose config check, a Trivy image scan, and smoke tests. build-push.yml is manual-trigger only: it builds images and pushes them to GHCR, and does not deploy; its header says the normal flow is build on the server. Outside Moksy, ggsocial runs only its Postgres in Docker (127.0.0.1:5434, with a named volume), while the app itself runs under PM2.

questions.prompt: What does marking the moksy-internal network as internal: true do?

options.text: It encrypts all traffic between containers
It exposes every container port publicly
Containers on it cannot reach the outside world
It makes the network faster
As the reverse proxy on the production VPS
Inside the dashboard container image, serving the compiled static files
As the load balancer in front of Kubernetes
As the TLS terminator for ggmoney

questions.prompt: What does Moksy's build-push.yml workflow do?

options.text: Is run by hand and pushes images to GHCR without deploying anything
Deploys to production on every push to main
Runs the unit tests on pull requests
Applies the Kubernetes manifests

questions.prompt: A container in the Moksy compose file occasionally exits cleanly (code 0) and the site stays down until someone notices. Which restart policy would you choose and why, and what else in our pipeline helps catch image problems before they run?
questions.answer: Use restart: unless-stopped, because on-failure only restarts on non-zero exit codes, so a clean exit is never retried. Before running, ci.yml validates the Compose config and scans production images with Trivy, and uses lint, unit, integration and smoke jobs to catch broken builds early.
questions.rubric: Chooses unless-stopped and explains exit code 0 versus on-failure; mentions CI image scan or compose config check.

items.title: Kubernetes, Terraform and Nginx: used, config only, or absent
items.body: Be exact about what we use. Used in production: Apache, certbot, PM2, Cloudflare, Docker (ggsocial's Postgres, Moksy's compose stack) and one GitHub Actions deploy workflow in gglearn. Present only as configuration: Moksy has a k8s/base folder with a gateway Deployment (two replicas, CPU and memory requests and limits, readiness probe), a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, an Ingress, a NetworkPolicy and a PodDisruptionBudget. We found no sign that a cluster runs them, and Moksy's own build-push header says the real flow is build on the server with Compose. It also has an observability folder with Loki and Promtail configs and an alert-dispatcher script; whether they run in production is not shown by the repo. Catalogued only: Moksy's integrations list names Kubernetes and Terraform as integrations at a with-a-script level, meaning something Moksy could connect to for customers, not tooling we operate. Absent: no Terraform .tf files exist in any repo we searched, and none of the VPS apps use Nginx or Kubernetes. A good rule when someone asks about a tool: say run, configured, catalogued or absent. Choose Kubernetes when you need many services scaled and healed automatically; for one VPS with three apps, Compose plus PM2 is far less to operate.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes moving gglearn, ggsocial and ggmoney to Kubernetes with Terraform because it is 'industry standard'. Using what our repos show, write a balanced recommendation.
questions.answer: Our current setup is one VPS with Apache, certbot, PM2, Cloudflare and a scripted deploy, which three small apps handle with little to operate. Kubernetes manifests exist only for the Moksy gateway and no cluster use is evidenced, and there are no Terraform files, so the team has no operating experience to build on. Kubernetes pays off with many services needing autoscaling and self-healing (Moksy may), but for these apps it adds cost and complexity. Recommend keeping the current stack, improving it (add tests to gglearn's workflow, backups), and revisiting if load or service count grows.
questions.rubric: Distinguishes used, config-only, absent; weighs complexity against need; refers to the evidence; gives a clear recommendation and a trigger to revisit.
